title: Language classes, pumping lemmas and closure

chapter_note.about: This chapter places languages in the hierarchy and gives the tools to prove where they belong. It starts with the chain Regular, DCFL, CFL, CSL, recursive, RE, and with classifying a language by the memory a machine needs. The two pumping lemmas then show how to prove that a language is not regular or not context-free, and Myhill-Nerode gives the exact test for regularity. The rest is closure properties for each class and decision properties (what an algorithm can answer). Most questions give four languages and ask which are regular or context-free.
chapter_note.simple: Different word patterns need machines of different power. A pattern like 'an even number of a's' needs only a tiny memory, matching brackets needs a pile of plates, three things that must agree need more, and some questions cannot be answered by any machine at all. This chapter teaches you to look at a pattern and say how much memory it needs, and to prove a pattern is too hard for a smaller machine using the pumping trick (repeat a part of a long word and see what breaks). It also teaches which operations on patterns keep you inside the same family, and which questions about a pattern a program can always answer. In exam words: hierarchy, classification, pumping lemmas, Myhill-Nerode, closure and decision properties.

cards.title: Language hierarchy
cards.simple: Think of a set of Russian dolls, where each bigger doll can do everything the smaller one can and a bit more. The smallest doll is a machine that only remembers a few fixed things, like a turnstile. The next one adds a pile of plates, then a pile it can guess with, then a long strip of paper it can write on, and the biggest ones are full computers. Each extra tool lets the machine recognise more kinds of words, and for every step there is a famous word pattern that the smaller doll cannot handle but the bigger one can. In exam words: Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ recursive ⊂ RE, and each inclusion is strict.
cards.idea: Languages form a **hierarchy** by the memory a machine needs. Finite memory gives regular languages, one stack gives context-free ones, a tape as long as the input gives context-sensitive ones, and a full Turing machine gives recursive and recursively enumerable ones. Each class sits strictly inside the next.
cards.definition:
Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ Recursive ⊂ RE, with every inclusion strict.

- Regular: DFA, NFA, regular expression (finite memory).
- DCFL: deterministic PDA. CFL: PDA or context-free grammar.
- CSL: linear bounded automaton, rules α → β with |α| ≤ |β|.
- Recursive (decidable): a Turing machine that always halts. RE: a Turing machine that halts on exactly the strings of the language.

Standard witnesses: aⁿbⁿ (DCFL, not regular), w wᴿ (CFL, not DCFL), aⁿbⁿcⁿ and w w (CSL, not CFL), the halting language (RE, not recursive).
cards.intuition_full: Each step gives the machine one extra resource. A stack remembers an unbounded count but can compare only one thing, because reading the stack back destroys it. A tape can be rewritten and revisited, so it can compare two counts or copy a string. A machine allowed to run forever can search without stopping, so it can confirm membership but may never rule it out. The witnesses show each step is real. The hierarchy gives a quick test: to place a language, ask what a machine must remember, and use the smallest class that fits. Regular languages are also DCFLs, and every language in a class is also in all bigger classes.

examples.setup: Walk outward through the hierarchy and, for each class, name a language that is in it but not in the class just inside.
steps: Languages are sorted by the memory needed to recognise them. Innermost: regular languages, which need only finite memory. A typical member is a*b*.
Add one stack, used deterministically: DCFL. The language aⁿbⁿ is a DCFL but not regular, so the inclusion Regular ⊂ DCFL is strict.
Let the stack machine guess: CFL. The language w wᴿ (even palindromes) is context-free but not deterministic, so DCFL ⊂ CFL is strict.
Give the machine a tape as long as the input: context-sensitive (CSL). The language aⁿbⁿcⁿ needs two comparisons at once, so it is CSL but not CF.
Allow a Turing machine that always halts: recursive. By diagonalisation there are decidable languages that no length-bounded machine can decide.
Allow a Turing machine that may run forever: RE. The halting language is RE but not recursive. Chain: Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ Recursive ⊂ RE, every inclusion strict.
examples.answer: a*b* (regular), aⁿbⁿ (DCFL, not regular), w wᴿ (CFL, not DCFL), aⁿbⁿcⁿ (CSL, not CF), a decidable diagonal language (recursive, not CSL), halting (RE, not recursive).

cards.title: Classify by memory
cards.simple: To decide how powerful a machine you need for a word pattern, ask what it must keep in its head. If it only has to remember something small, like whether the number so far is odd or even, a very simple machine is enough. If it has to match one block against another block, like the same number of opening and closing brackets, a pile of plates works, as long as the matches are nested like brackets. If the matches cross over each other, or three things must agree, one pile is not enough. In exam words: finite memory is regular, one stack is context-free for nested pairs, crossing pairs and three tied counts are context-sensitive, and a unary language is regular only if its lengths are ultimately periodic.
cards.idea: To classify a language, ask **what a machine must remember**. A modulus or a bounded count is finite memory: **regular**. Draw an arc between blocks that must match: nested arcs need one stack (**context-free**), while crossing arcs, three tied counts or a copy w w need more (**context-sensitive**).
cards.definition:
Rules of thumb for languages over blocks aⁿbᵐ…:

- Counts compared only modulo a constant, or kept within a fixed distance: regular.
- Two counts compared, with nested dependencies (aⁿbⁿ, aⁿbᵐcᵐdⁿ, w wᴿ, aⁿbᵐcⁿ⁺ᵐ): context-free.
- Three counts compared (aⁿbⁿcⁿ), crossing dependencies (aⁿbᵐcⁿdᵐ) or copies (w w): context-sensitive, not CF.
- Unary languages: regular if the set of lengths is ultimately periodic, otherwise not even CF (examples: primes, squares, powers of 2).
- A language like w x wᴿ with non-empty parts only forces first = last, so it is regular.
cards.intuition_full: One stack remembers a sequence in order and gives it back in reverse. That matches a nested structure perfectly: the last thing opened is the first closed. A crossing structure needs the oldest item first, which the stack buries. Three tied counts need two comparisons from the same stack. For a unary language the stack is no better than a counter, and a counter that checks a single count is still periodic, which is why a unary CF language is regular. When in doubt, replace the language by the plainest condition it expresses and ask what a machine would have to remember to check it. Always check for a modulus first: it keeps languages regular.

examples.setup: Classify three languages by memory: L1 = {aⁿbᵐcᵐdⁿ}, L2 = {aⁿbᵐcⁿdᵐ}, and L3 = {aⁿbᵐ : n + m is even}.
steps: Ask what memory a language needs. Find the blocks whose lengths must match, and draw an arc between each tied pair. The shape of the arcs decides the class.
L1 = aⁿbᵐcᵐdⁿ: the arcs a-d and b-c are nested. The inner pair is finished before the outer one, so one stack handles it. L1 is context-free.
L2 = aⁿbᵐcⁿdᵐ: the arcs a-c and b-d cross. After pushing the a's and then the b's, the a's are buried under the b's, so one stack cannot reach them. L2 is context-sensitive, not context-free.
L3 = aⁿbᵐ with n + m even: there is no arc, only a parity to remember. Finite memory suffices, so L3 is regular.
Unary languages are special: a context-free language over one letter is regular, so it is regular exactly when its length set is ultimately periodic. Primes are not, so {aᵖ : p prime} is not even CF.
Summary: nested pairs are CF, crossing pairs or three tied counts are CSL, a modulus or a bounded count is regular.
examples.answer: L1 is context-free (nested arcs), L2 is context-sensitive and not CF (crossing arcs), L3 is regular (only a parity).

examples.setup: Which of these languages is not context-free? (A) {aⁿbᵐ : n ≥ m}  (B) {aⁿbᵐcⁿ⁺ᵐ}  (C) {aⁿ b^(n²)}  (D) {w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) = 2 · #b(w)}
steps: (A) Push the a's, pop one per b, and accept with a's left over. One stack: context-free.
(B) aⁿbᵐcⁿ⁺ᵐ = aⁿ (bᵐcᵐ) cⁿ: the b-c pair sits inside the a-c pair. Nested, so context-free.
(C) The b-block must have length n², not a multiple or a sum of n. A stack can compare lengths 1 to 1 or 1 to 2, but cannot square. Not context-free.
(D) Push or pop so that every b is worth two a's. A stack with the right bookkeeping handles it: context-free.
examples.answer: (C) {aⁿ b^(n²)} is not context-free.

examples.setup: Is L = {aⁿ : n is even or n ≥ 7} regular?
steps: It is a unary language, so look at the length set {0, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, …}.
From 7 on every length is in L, so the set is ultimately periodic (period 1 after 7).
A DFA counts the length up to 6 and from then on accepts everything. Brute force confirms that its minimal DFA has 7 states.
examples.answer: Regular. An ultimately periodic length set gives a regular unary language, even if it looks irregular at the start.

cards.title: Pumping lemma for regular languages
cards.simple: Suppose a machine with only a few squares reads a really long word. It must walk through the same square twice, which means there is a loop it went round in the middle of the word. If it went round the loop once, it could just as well go round it twice, or not at all, and still end on the same final square. So any word the machine accepts can have that loop part repeated or deleted and still be accepted. To prove a language is not regular, you show that repeating some part of a long word ruins it. In exam words: the pumping lemma says long words in a regular language split as xyz with |xy| ≤ p and |y| ≥ 1, and x yⁱ z stays in the language for all i ≥ 0; it can refute regularity but never prove it.
cards.idea: If a language is regular, every **long enough word** in it has a middle piece y that can be repeated or deleted without leaving the language. To prove a language is **not** regular, pick a long word, note that y must lie in the first p letters, and show that pumping y breaks the language.
cards.definition:
Pumping lemma (regular): if L is regular there is a number p ≥ 1 such that every w in L with |w| ≥ p can be written w = xyz with

- |xy| ≤ p,
- |y| ≥ 1,
- x yⁱ z in L for every i ≥ 0.

Use it to refute: assume L is regular, pick w = aᵖbᵖ (or similar) so that |xy| ≤ p traps y in one block, pick i = 0 or 2, show x yⁱ z is not in L. It is a necessary condition only: some non-regular languages satisfy it.
cards.intuition_full: A DFA with p states reading p or more letters must repeat a state, so the path contains a loop. The part of the word read around that loop is y. Going round the loop 0, 2, 3, … times gives other words that end in the same state, so they are accepted too. The condition |xy| ≤ p holds because the first repeated state appears within the first p letters. In a proof, choose w so that the first p letters are all in one block (all a's). Then y is a block of a's whatever the split, and pumping changes only one of the two counts. The lemma is one-directional: failing it proves non-regularity, passing it proves nothing.

examples.setup: Use the pumping lemma to show that L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not regular. Illustrate with p = 4 and w = aaaabbbb.
steps: Claim: L = {aⁿbⁿ} is not regular. Suppose it is, with pumping length p. Choose w = aᵖbᵖ. To see it, take p = 4: w = aaaabbbb.
The lemma splits w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p and |y| ≥ 1. Since |xy| ≤ 4, both x and y lie inside the first four letters, which are all a's.
Take one possible split: x = a, y = aa, z = abbbb. The lemma says xyⁱz must stay in L for every i ≥ 0.
Pump y once more (i = 2): x y y z = a + aaaa + abbbb. The a-block grows from 4 to 6 and the b-block stays at 4.
Now there are 6 a's and 4 b's, so xy²z = aaaaaabbbb is not in L. This contradicts the lemma.
Every split fails the same way: y is a non-empty block of a's, so pumping changes the a count but not the b count. So no pumping length exists, and L is not regular.
Careful: the lemma can only refute regularity. Some non-regular languages can be pumped, so passing the test never proves a language regular.
examples.answer: Every split x y z of aᵖbᵖ with |xy| ≤ p has y = aᵏ with k ≥ 1, and x y² z has more a's than b's. So L is not regular.

examples.setup: L = {a^(6+3k) : k ≥ 0} is regular. What is the smallest pumping length p for L?
steps: Members have lengths 6, 9, 12, …. A pumping length p must work for every member of length at least p.
Try p = 6. The member a⁶ has length 6 ≥ p, and removing any non-empty y (i = 0) leaves a string of length at most 5, which is not in L. So p = 6, and every smaller p, fails.
Try p = 7. Members of length at least 7 are a⁹, a¹², …. Take x = ε and y = aaa. Removing y gives a⁶, which is in L, and adding copies of y keeps the length at least 6 and divisible by 3.

cards.title: Pumping lemma for CFLs
cards.simple: For a context-free language, a long word has two parts that can be repeated together, like pumping both ends of a sandwich at once. The catch is that the two parts live inside a short window of the word. In a word like aaabbbccc, a short window can reach only one or two of the three letter groups, so repeating its parts changes two counts at most and leaves the third alone. The three counts are no longer equal, so the new word is not in the language. In exam words: long words split as uvxyz with |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| ≥ 1, and u vⁱ x yⁱ z stays in the language for all i ≥ 0; to refute context-freeness you show that a short window misses a letter group.
cards.idea: If a language is context-free, every long word can be split into **u v x y z**, with the pumpable pieces v and y both inside a **short window** vxy. Repeating v and y together keeps the word in the language. To refute context-freeness, choose a word where any short window misses a whole letter group, so pumping breaks the balance of counts.
cards.definition:
Pumping lemma (CFL): if L is context-free there is p ≥ 1 such that every w in L with |w| ≥ p can be written w = u v x y z with

- |vxy| ≤ p,
- |vy| ≥ 1,
- u vⁱ x yⁱ z in L for every i ≥ 0.

Proof recipe: assume L is CF, choose w = aᵖbᵖcᵖ (or similar), argue that vxy touches at most two blocks, and show some i (0 or 2) breaks the language. Like the regular lemma, it can refute but never prove.
cards.intuition_full: A parse tree of a very long word is deep, so some variable A repeats on a path. The part derived from the upper A contains the part derived from the lower A, which gives w = u v x y z with v and y generated around the repeated variable. Repeating that step pumps v and y together. Because the repeated variable is near the bottom of the tree, the window vxy is short: it has at most p letters. In aᵖbᵖcᵖ, the blocks are each p long, so a window of p letters reaches at most two blocks. Pumping changes at most two counts and leaves the third, which breaks aⁿbⁿcⁿ.

examples.setup: Use the pumping lemma for context-free languages to show that L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not context-free. Illustrate with p = 3 and w = aaabbbccc.
steps: Claim: L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is not context-free. Suppose it is, with pumping length p. Choose w = aᵖbᵖcᵖ. For p = 3 that is aaabbbccc.
The lemma splits w = uvxyz with |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| ≥ 1. The last a and the first c are 4 apart, so a window of at most 3 letters cannot touch both. It misses a whole letter group.
Case 1: the window lies inside one block. Take v = a and y = a, the second and third letters, with x empty.
Pump up (i = 2): u v v x y y z has 5 a's, 3 b's and 3 c's. Only the a's grew, so it is not in L.
Case 2: the window straddles two blocks. Take v = the last a, x = b, y = the next b (letters 3 to 5).
Pump up (i = 2): u v v x y y z has 4 a's, 4 b's and still 3 c's. The c's did not change, so it is not in L.
Every window misses at least one letter group, so pumping breaks the equal counts every time (checked by search for p = 2 to 5). Contradiction: L is not context-free.
examples.answer: Any window vxy of at most p letters misses a block, so pumping changes at most two of the three counts. The result is not in L, so L is not context-free.

examples.setup: Show that L = {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i < j < k} is not context-free by choosing the word w = aᵖbᵖ⁺¹cᵖ⁺².
steps: A window vxy of at most p letters touches at most two of the three blocks, so one block keeps its length.
If vy lies only in the a's, pump up (i = 2): the a count rises to at least p + 1, which is not less than the b count p + 1. Not in L.

If vy lies only in the b's, pump up: the b count reaches p + 2 or more, which is not less than the c count p + 2. If vy lies only in the c's, pump down (i = 0): the c count falls to at most p + 1, not more than the b count.

If vy touches two blocks, pumping up raises the earlier block as well as the later one, or pumping down lowers one of them, so the strict order i < j < k fails. A search over every split for p = 2 to 4 confirms that i = 0 or i = 2 always breaks the order.
examples.answer: L is not context-free. The word aᵖbᵖ⁺¹cᵖ⁺² has no pumpable window.

examples.setup: Show that L = {aᵖ : p is a prime number} is not context-free.
steps: Take a prime q larger than p + 1 and w = a^q. Then v = aᵃ and y = aᵇ with a + b = k, where 1 ≤ k ≤ p.
The word with v and y pumped i times has length q + (i − 1)k. Let m = q − k be the length of u x z, which is at least 2.
Choose i = m: the new length is m + m k = m (1 + k), a product of two numbers that are at least 2, so it is composite.
A composite length is not in L, which contradicts the lemma. A numeric search over primes up to 80 and every k confirms it.
examples.answer: L is not context-free. The pumped length m(1 + k) is always composite.

cards.title: Closure of regular languages
cards.simple: Regular languages are like a very well-behaved club: if you take members and do certain things to them, the result is always a member too. You can combine two of them with 'or' or 'and', flip yes to no, read the words backwards, chop off the end of every word, or chop off the start. Reading backwards is easy to picture on the machine: you turn every arrow around and swap where you start and where you finish. The things that break the club are doing infinitely many unions or taking a random chunk of the language. In exam words: regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation, star, reversal, prefix and suffix, but not under infinite union or arbitrary subsets.
cards.idea: Regular languages are **closed** under all the usual operations: union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation, star, **reversal, prefix and suffix**. Each has a construction on automata. They are not closed under infinite union or under taking an arbitrary subset.
cards.intuition_full: Every construction works because a DFA has finitely many states, so any new rule only needs finitely many extra bits of memory. Reversal reads the machine backwards. Prefix needs only to know whether the future can still reach a final state, which is a property of the current state. For {x : xx in L}, a finite machine can track, for each possible starting state q, where x would lead from q, and that is a finite table. To refute a closure claim, test extreme languages: take L = ∅ or L = Σ*, or a non-regular language such as aⁿbⁿ. If a union of two languages is regular, that says nothing about each part: the complement of aⁿbⁿ unions with aⁿbⁿ to make Σ*.

examples.setup: A DFA M accepts L = a b* c. Build a machine for the reversal of L and test it on cbba.
steps: M accepts L = a b* c: an a, then any number of b's, then a c. State s0 is the start and s2 is the only final state.
To reverse the language, flip every arrow. The arrow s0 → s1 on a becomes s1 → s0 on a, and likewise for the others. The loop stays.
Swap the roles of the ends: the old final state s2 becomes the new start, and the old start s0 becomes the new final state.
Run the new machine on cbba, which is abbc reversed: s2 reads c to s1, reads b twice and stays in s1, reads a to s0. It ends in a final state, so cbba is accepted.
In general flipping arrows turns a DFA into an NFA, because several final states become several start states. Determinise afterwards: the state count can grow, up to 2^k.
So regular languages are closed under reversal, together with union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation, star, prefix and suffix.
examples.answer: Flip all arrows, make s2 the start and s0 the final state. It accepts c b* a, and cbba is accepted.

examples.setup: L is regular. Which must be regular? (i) prefix(L) = {x : xy in L for some y}  (ii) {x : xx in L}  (iii) L ∩ Lᴿ  (iv) {x in L : |x| is prime}
steps: (i) In a DFA for L, make every state that can reach a final state final. The new machine accepts exactly the prefixes. Regular.

(ii) Run one copy of the DFA from every state at the same time. After reading x, the table 'state reached from q' tells whether xx ∈ L, because x starts in q0, ends in q = δ(q0, x), and needs δ(q, x) final. There are finitely many tables, so it is regular. A check on a random 4-state DFA agreed with this construction on every string up to length 8.
(iii) Lᴿ is regular and regular languages are closed under intersection. Regular.
(iv) Take L = Σ*. Then the set is the words whose length is prime, which is not regular. Not necessarily regular.
examples.answer: (i), (ii) and (iii) must be regular. (iv) need not be.

cards.title: Closure of other classes
cards.simple: Each family of languages has things you can do to it without leaving the family, and a few things that throw you out. Think of it as a table with a row for each family and a column for each operation, and a tick or a cross in each box. Regular families tick everything. The pile-of-plates family loses 'both at once' and 'flip yes and no'. The simplest family of full computers loses 'flip yes and no', because a machine that sometimes runs forever can say 'yes' but may never be able to say 'no'. You mostly need to remember the crosses. In exam words: CFLs are not closed under intersection or complement, DCFLs are closed under complement but not union, RE is not closed under complement, and recursive and context-sensitive languages are closed under complement.
cards.idea: Closure facts differ by class, so memorise the **'no' cells**. **CFL** is not closed under intersection or complement, **DCFL** is closed under complement only, and **RE** is not closed under complement, while **recursive** and **CSL** are closed under complement.
cards.definition:
Closure under union, intersection, complement, concatenation and star:

- Regular: all five.
- DCFL: complement only (also intersection with a regular language).
- CFL: union, concatenation, star (not intersection, not complement).
- CSL: all five (complement by Immerman-Szelepcsényi).
- Recursive: all five.
- RE: union, intersection, concatenation, star (not complement).

Tests: rewrite with De Morgan; try L = ∅ and L = Σ*; use aⁿbⁿcⁿ = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} ∩ {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} and the halting language.
cards.intuition_full: Complement is the sensitive operation. A DFA or a deterministic machine that always halts can flip its answer, so complement is safe for regular, DCFL, recursive and CSL. A non-deterministic stack machine cannot flip a 'some branch accepts' answer, and an RE machine that runs forever cannot flip 'never halts' into 'accepts'. Intersection fails for CFLs because two stacks are needed, and for DCFLs for the same reason. Union fails for DCFLs because merging two deterministic machines forces a guess. If both a language and its complement are RE, run both machines side by side: one must halt, which makes the language decidable.

examples.setup: Fill the closure table for the six classes and five operations (union, intersection, complement, concatenation, star), giving a reason for each 'no'.
steps: For each class, which of five operations keep you inside it? The cells that matter are the 'no' ones. We fill the table class by class.
Regular: closed under all five. Each has a construction on DFAs and NFAs.
DCFL: only complement survives (a DPDA can be completed and its answer flipped). Union fails: {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j} ∪ {aⁱbʲcᵏ : j = k} needs a guess.
CFL: union, concatenation and star combine grammars. Intersection and complement fail, because {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} ∩ {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}.
CSL: closed under all five. Closure under complement is the Immerman-Szelepcsényi theorem: nondeterministic linear space is closed under complement.
Recursive: closed under all five. For complement, run the decider and swap accept with reject.
RE: closed under all but complement. If both L and its complement were RE, L would be recursive, and the halting language is RE but not recursive.
Seven 'no' cells to remember: DCFL has four (union, intersection, concatenation, star), CFL has two (intersection, complement), RE has one (complement).
examples.answer: The seven 'no' cells: DCFL (union, intersection, concatenation, star), CFL (intersection, complement), RE (complement). Everything else is closed.

examples.setup: L is recursively enumerable and so is its complement. What can you say about L?
steps: Take a Turing machine M1 that halts exactly on strings in L, and M2 that halts exactly on strings not in L.
On input w run M1 and M2 alternately, one step each. Exactly one of them will halt, because w is either in L or not.
If M1 halts, accept. If M2 halts, reject. This always halts, so it decides L.
Hence L is recursive. Equivalently, a language that is RE but not recursive, like halting, has a complement that is not RE.
examples.answer: L is recursive.

examples.setup: The complement of {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} over {a, b, c} is context-free, yet {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is not. Does this contradict the fact that CFLs are not closed under complement?
steps: Closure under complement means: for every L in the class, the complement is in the class. One counterexample breaks it, and the counterexample must start inside the class.
Take L = the complement of aⁿbⁿcⁿ. A PDA can accept it by guessing that the order is wrong or that one of the three counts differs. So L is a CFL.
The complement of L is aⁿbⁿcⁿ, which is not a CFL. So L is exactly a CFL whose complement leaves the class.
examples.answer: No contradiction. It is the counterexample: L is a CFL and its complement aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not.

connections: The CFL closure card in the grammar chapter gives the proofs for union and the failure of intersection.

cards.title: Decision properties
cards.simple: Some questions about a language can be answered by a program that always finishes with yes or no, and some cannot. For the simplest kinds of machines, almost every sensible question has such a program, because the machine is so small that you can check all its behaviour. For grammars, you can still ask whether it makes any word at all, by working out which of its parts can eventually turn into plain letters. But for questions like 'do two grammars make exactly the same words', no program can always give the right answer. In exam words: for regular languages every standard problem is decidable, and for CFGs membership, emptiness and finiteness are decidable while equivalence, universality and ambiguity are undecidable.
cards.idea: A problem is **decidable** if some algorithm always halts with the right yes or no. For **regular** languages every standard question is decidable. For **context-free grammars** you can decide membership, emptiness and finiteness, but not equivalence, universality (is L = Σ*?), ambiguity, or whether two CFGs share a word. To test emptiness, mark the variables that can produce a terminal string until nothing changes.
cards.intuition_full: A question is decidable when a bounded search always settles it. Emptiness of a CFG works because a derivation that uses a variable twice on one path can be shortened: if S can derive any terminal string at all, it can do so with a derivation tree of bounded height. The marking procedure is just a fixed point over that finite set. Finiteness follows from the pumping lemma: if the language has a string of length between p and 2p, it is infinite. Equivalence and universality of CFGs, in contrast, can encode the halting of Turing machines, so no algorithm exists. For regular languages the product and complement constructions turn every question into reachability in a finite graph.

examples.setup: G: S → AB, A → aA | C, B → bB | b, C → CC. Decide whether L(G) is empty, then repeat after changing A → C into A → a.
steps: Is L(G) empty? G: S → AB, A → aA | C, B → bB | b, C → CC. Emptiness is decidable. Mark a variable if some rule for it uses only terminals and already marked variables, and repeat until nothing changes. The arrows show which variables each variable needs.
Round 1: B → b uses only a terminal, so B can produce a string. Mark B.
Round 2: A → aA needs A, which is not marked, and A → C needs C, which is not marked. C → CC needs C. S → AB needs A. Nothing new is marked, so we have reached a fixed point.
S is not marked, so S derives no terminal string. L(G) = ∅. A search over all derivations up to length 8 finds no string, which agrees.
Change A → C into A → a. Round 1 now marks A and B, since both have terminal-only rules. Round 2: S → AB uses two marked variables, so S is marked. L(G) is not empty and contains ab.

The same fixed-point style decides finiteness, and CYK decides membership. Equivalence, universality and ambiguity of context-free grammars are undecidable, and so is almost everything about Turing machines.
examples.answer: L(G) is empty, because S never gets marked. After the change, A, B and then S are marked, so L(G) is not empty.

examples.setup: G: S → AB, A → a, B → CD | b, C → c, D → d. Is L(G) finite? Compare with S → AB, A → AA | a, B → b.
steps: Finiteness is decidable. First remove useless symbols (those that generate nothing or cannot be reached). Here every symbol is useful.
Draw the dependency graph: an arrow X → Y when Y appears on the right of a rule for X. Here S → A, S → B, B → C and B → D.
A grammar in CNF generates an infinite language exactly when this graph has a cycle through useful variables, since a cycle lets derivations grow without limit. This graph has no cycle.
So L(G) is finite: S ⇒ AB ⇒ aB ⇒ ab and S ⇒ AB ⇒ aB ⇒ aCD ⇒ acD ⇒ acd. In S → AB, A → AA | a, B → b, the loop A → A makes the language {aⁿb : n ≥ 1} infinite.
examples.answer: L(G) = {ab, acd} is finite. A cycle in the dependency graph would make it infinite.

examples.setup: D is a DFA over {a, b} for strings with no bb. Is L(D) = Σ* (universality)? Why is this decidable for DFAs but not for CFGs?
steps: Complement the DFA: flip final and non-final states. The new DFA accepts exactly the strings that D rejects.
L(D) = Σ* if and only if the complement accepts nothing, which is a reachability question: can a final state be reached from the start state?
Here the complement reaches its final state by reading bb, so bb is rejected by D and L(D) ≠ Σ*.
For CFGs no such complement exists (CFLs are not closed under complement), and universality is undecidable.
examples.answer: L(D) ≠ Σ*, with witness bb. Universality is decidable for regular languages through complement and reachability.

cards.why: Decision problems for languages are asked together with the hierarchy and with TM undecidability. In GATE: which of several problems on CFGs is undecidable, or which problems on DFAs are decidable.
how: For regular languages answer 'decidable' for all standard problems.
For a CFG, recall the three decidable ones: membership, emptiness, finiteness.
Everything else (equivalence, universality, ambiguity, intersection emptiness, regularity) is undecidable.
For Turing machines apply Rice's theorem to any non-trivial property of the language.
cards.mistake: Assuming a problem is decidable because the machine is small. Equivalence and universality of CFGs are undecidable even though CFGs are far weaker than Turing machines. The opposite slip is to claim emptiness of a CFG is undecidable: it has a simple fixed-point algorithm.
edge_cases: Membership for a CSL is decidable (bounded tape) but PSPACE-hard.
'Is L(G) regular?' is undecidable for CFGs, even though regular languages are CFLs.
Equivalence of two DPDAs is decidable, a deep theorem beyond the syllabus.
connections: Rice's theorem and reductions (next chapter) explain why every non-trivial TM property is undecidable.
The closure card gives the reason: complement is not available for CFLs, so universality cannot reduce to emptiness.

check.q: Is it decidable whether a CFG generates the empty language?
check.a: Yes. Mark the variables that generate terminal strings and check whether S is marked.

check.q: Is ambiguity of CFGs decidable?
check.a: No.

check.q: Is equality of two regular expressions decidable?
check.a: Yes. Compare DFAs through the product and test emptiness of the symmetric difference.

cards.title: Myhill-Nerode and drift
cards.simple: A machine with only a few squares can keep only a few different memories. So if you can find lots of different starts of words that need lots of different follow-ups, the machine would need lots of different memories, one for each. For the words aⁿbⁿ, the start 'aaa' needs exactly three b's later, and the start 'aa' needs exactly two, so every start needs its own memory. Since there are infinitely many starts, no machine with a fixed number of squares can do it. If the thing you have to remember stays small, like how far ahead you are by at most one, a few squares are enough. In exam words: a language is regular exactly when it has finitely many classes of indistinguishable prefixes (Myhill-Nerode), and counts that cannot drift far apart give a regular language.
cards.idea: Two prefixes are **distinguishable** if some suffix accepts one and not the other. A language is regular exactly when the number of classes of prefixes is **finite** (this is Myhill-Nerode). If you find infinitely many pairwise distinguishable prefixes, the language is not regular. If the counts you compare can only **drift** a bounded amount apart, a finite memory suffices.
cards.definition:
For a language L, prefixes u and v are equivalent if for every suffix z: uz ∈ L ⇔ vz ∈ L. The classes are the Myhill-Nerode classes.

- L is regular ⇔ the number of classes is finite, and then it equals the number of states of the minimal DFA.
- To refute regularity: give infinitely many prefixes u1, u2, … and for each pair i ≠ j a suffix that separates them.
- Drift: if two counts are compared only while their difference stays within a fixed bound (for example |#a − #b| ≤ 1 at every prefix), the difference takes finitely many values, and the language is regular.
cards.intuition_full: A DFA state is a promise about the future, and equivalent prefixes make the same promise. If a language needs infinitely many different promises, no finite machine can keep them. For aⁿbⁿ the prefix aⁱ promises 'exactly i more b's', which is a different promise for every i. Compare that with a language where you only need to know the current difference of two counts and the difference is trapped between −1 and +1: there are three promises and a dead state, which is finite. The pumping lemma proves the same facts through a more indirect route. Myhill-Nerode is stronger: it also proves regularity when the classes are finite.

examples.setup: Use Myhill-Nerode to show that L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not regular. Tabulate the prefixes ε, a, aa, aaa, aaaa against the suffixes ε, b, bb, bbb, bbbb.
steps: Two prefixes u and v are distinguishable if some suffix z puts exactly one of uz, vz in L. A regular language has only finitely many classes of prefixes. Test L = {aⁿbⁿ}: each row is a prefix aⁱ, each column a suffix bʲ, and a cell is 1 when aⁱbʲ is in L.
Row ε: εbʲ = bʲ is in L only when j = 0, so the row is 1 0 0 0 0.
Row a: abʲ is in L only when j = 1, so the row is 0 1 0 0 0.
Row aa: aabʲ is in L only when j = 2, so the 1 moves one place right.
Rows aaa and aaaa: the 1 sits at j = 3 and j = 4. Every row has its 1 in a different column.
All five rows are different, so ε, a, aa, aaa, aaaa are pairwise distinguishable: the 1s form a diagonal.
Continue the rows without limit: every new prefix aⁱ gets its own column bⁱ. That gives infinitely many classes, but a DFA with k states can only separate k prefixes. So L is not regular.
examples.answer: Each prefix aⁱ is separated from every other by the suffix bⁱ, so there are infinitely many classes and L is not regular.

examples.setup: Is L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) = #b(w)} regular?
steps: Take the prefixes aⁱ for i = 0, 1, 2, ….
For i ≠ j, the suffix bⁱ gives aⁱbⁱ, which has equal counts and is in L, but aʲbⁱ has different counts and is not in L.
So the prefixes are pairwise distinguishable: infinitely many classes.
A regular language has finitely many classes, so L is not regular. The closure argument agrees: L ∩ a*b* = {aⁿbⁿ}, which is not regular.
examples.answer: Not regular.

examples.setup: Now require that every prefix of w has |#a − #b| ≤ 1 as well as #a(w) = #b(w). Is that language regular?
steps: The difference #a − #b of a prefix can only be −1, 0 or +1. Any move that would reach ±2 breaks the rule.
So a finite memory suffices: three values of the difference plus a dead state for violations.
From difference 0 the next symbol moves it to ±1 and the one after must bring it back to 0, so the words are blocks ab or ba: (ab + ba)*.
A brute-force check of all strings up to length 12 confirms that this language equals (ab + ba)*.
examples.answer: Regular, equal to (ab + ba)*. Counts that stay close together are finite memory, even though they compare two counts.

cards.why: This is the sharpest tool for 'is it regular?' questions, and the drift idea explains why some count-comparing languages are still regular. In GATE: decide regularity for languages that compare counts or that depend on how far counts drift.
how: Look for an infinite family of prefixes that need different futures (aⁱ and bⁱ).
Show a suffix that separates every pair.
If the compared counts stay within a bounded difference, list the finitely many states instead.
Cross-check with the pumping lemma or with closure (intersect with a*b*).
cards.mistake: Calling a language non-regular just because it compares two counts. If the counts can only drift a bounded amount, the difference takes finitely many values and the language is regular. The test is: how many different things must the machine remember?
edge_cases: The number of Myhill-Nerode classes equals the number of states of the minimal DFA.
A finite language has finitely many classes (the longest word bounds them).
Equal counts of a's and b's with no restriction on order is not regular, but equal counts with every prefix within 1 is.
connections: The pumping lemma for regular languages gives a one-way test, Myhill-Nerode gives an exact one.
Counting minimal DFA states (finite automata chapter) is counting these classes.

check.q: How many classes does a minimal DFA with 5 states have?
check.a: 5, one per state.

check.q: Which suffix separates the prefixes a³ and a⁵ for aⁿbⁿ?
check.a: b³: a³b³ is in L, a⁵b³ is not.

check.q: Is {w : |#a(w) − #b(w)| ≤ 2 for every prefix} regular?
check.a: Yes. The difference takes only five values.

cards.what_full:
Two prefixes are **distinguishable** if some suffix accepts one and not the other. A language is regular exactly when the number of classes of prefixes is **finite** (this is Myhill-Nerode). If you find infinitely many pairwise distinguishable prefixes, the language is not regular. If the counts you compare can only **drift** a bounded amount apart, a finite memory suffices.

For a language L, prefixes u and v are equivalent if for every suffix z: uz ∈ L ⇔ vz ∈ L. The classes are the Myhill-Nerode classes.

- L is regular ⇔ the number of classes is finite, and then it equals the number of states of the minimal DFA.
- To refute regularity: give infinitely many prefixes u1, u2, … and for each pair i ≠ j a suffix that separates them.
- Drift: if two counts are compared only while their difference stays within a fixed bound (for example |#a − #b| ≤ 1 at every prefix), the difference takes finitely many values, and the language is regular.

**Worked example.** Use Myhill-Nerode to show that L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not regular. Tabulate the prefixes ε, a, aa, aaa, aaaa against the suffixes ε, b, bb, bbb, bbbb.

1. Two prefixes u and v are distinguishable if some suffix z puts exactly one of uz, vz in L. A regular language has only finitely many classes of prefixes. Test L = {aⁿbⁿ}: each row is a prefix aⁱ, each column a suffix bʲ, and a cell is 1 when aⁱbʲ is in L.
2. Row ε: εbʲ = bʲ is in L only when j = 0, so the row is 1 0 0 0 0.
3. Row a: abʲ is in L only when j = 1, so the row is 0 1 0 0 0.
4. Row aa: aabʲ is in L only when j = 2, so the 1 moves one place right.
5. Rows aaa and aaaa: the 1 sits at j = 3 and j = 4. Every row has its 1 in a different column.
6. All five rows are different, so ε, a, aa, aaa, aaaa are pairwise distinguishable: the 1s form a diagonal.

This is the sharpest tool for 'is it regular?' questions, and the drift idea explains why some count-comparing languages are still regular. In GATE: decide regularity for languages that compare counts or that depend on how far counts drift.

scenes.title: The language hierarchy as nested circles

steps.caption: Languages are sorted by the memory needed to recognise them. Innermost: regular languages, which need only finite memory. A typical member is a*b*.
Add one stack, used deterministically: DCFL. The language aⁿbⁿ is a DCFL but not regular, so the inclusion Regular ⊂ DCFL is strict.
Let the stack machine guess: CFL. The language w wᴿ (even palindromes) is context-free but not deterministic, so DCFL ⊂ CFL is strict.
Give the machine a tape as long as the input: context-sensitive (CSL). The language aⁿbⁿcⁿ needs two comparisons at once, so it is CSL but not CF.
Allow a Turing machine that always halts: recursive. By diagonalisation there are decidable languages that no length-bounded machine can decide.
Allow a Turing machine that may run forever: RE. The halting language is RE but not recursive. Chain: Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ Recursive ⊂ RE, every inclusion strict.

scenes.title: Nested arcs are CF, crossing arcs are not

objects.text: aⁿbᵐ, n + m even : no arcs
unary primes aᵖ: not periodic, not CF
nested: CF   crossing: CSL   parity: REG

steps.caption: Ask what memory a language needs. Find the blocks whose lengths must match, and draw an arc between each tied pair. The shape of the arcs decides the class.
L1 = aⁿbᵐcᵐdⁿ: the arcs a-d and b-c are nested. The inner pair is finished before the outer one, so one stack handles it. L1 is context-free.
L2 = aⁿbᵐcⁿdᵐ: the arcs a-c and b-d cross. After pushing the a's and then the b's, the a's are buried under the b's, so one stack cannot reach them. L2 is context-sensitive, not context-free.
L3 = aⁿbᵐ with n + m even: there is no arc, only a parity to remember. Finite memory suffices, so L3 is regular.
Unary languages are special: a context-free language over one letter is regular, so it is regular exactly when its length set is ultimately periodic. Primes are not, so {aᵖ : p prime} is not even CF.
Summary: nested pairs are CF, crossing pairs or three tied counts are CSL, a modulus or a bounded count is regular.

scenes.title: Pumping a⁴b⁴ breaks the equal counts

steps.caption: Claim: L = {aⁿbⁿ} is not regular. Suppose it is, with pumping length p. Choose w = aᵖbᵖ. To see it, take p = 4: w = aaaabbbb.
The lemma splits w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p and |y| ≥ 1. Since |xy| ≤ 4, both x and y lie inside the first four letters, which are all a's.
Take one possible split: x = a, y = aa, z = abbbb. The lemma says xyⁱz must stay in L for every i ≥ 0.
Pump y once more (i = 2): x y y z = a + aaaa + abbbb. The a-block grows from 4 to 6 and the b-block stays at 4.
Now there are 6 a's and 4 b's, so xy²z = aaaaaabbbb is not in L. This contradicts the lemma.
Every split fails the same way: y is a non-empty block of a's, so pumping changes the a count but not the b count. So no pumping length exists, and L is not regular.
Careful: the lemma can only refute regularity. Some non-regular languages can be pumped, so passing the test never proves a language regular.

scenes.title: Pumping a³b³c³ breaks the counts in every case

steps.caption: Claim: L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is not context-free. Suppose it is, with pumping length p. Choose w = aᵖbᵖcᵖ. For p = 3 that is aaabbbccc.
The lemma splits w = uvxyz with |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| ≥ 1. The last a and the first c are 4 apart, so a window of at most 3 letters cannot touch both. It misses a whole letter group.
Case 1: the window lies inside one block. Take v = a and y = a, the second and third letters, with x empty.
Pump up (i = 2): u v v x y y z has 5 a's, 3 b's and 3 c's. Only the a's grew, so it is not in L.
Case 2: the window straddles two blocks. Take v = the last a, x = b, y = the next b (letters 3 to 5).
Pump up (i = 2): u v v x y y z has 4 a's, 4 b's and still 3 c's. The c's did not change, so it is not in L.
Every window misses at least one letter group, so pumping breaks the equal counts every time (checked by search for p = 2 to 5). Contradiction: L is not context-free.

scenes.title: Reversal: flip arrows, swap start and final

steps.caption: M accepts L = a b* c: an a, then any number of b's, then a c. State s0 is the start and s2 is the only final state.
To reverse the language, flip every arrow. The arrow s0 → s1 on a becomes s1 → s0 on a, and likewise for the others. The loop stays.
Swap the roles of the ends: the old final state s2 becomes the new start, and the old start s0 becomes the new final state.

set.text: start = old final, final = old start

steps.caption: Run the new machine on cbba, which is abbc reversed: s2 reads c to s1, reads b twice and stays in s1, reads a to s0. It ends in a final state, so cbba is accepted.
In general flipping arrows turns a DFA into an NFA, because several final states become several start states. Determinise afterwards: the state count can grow, up to 2^k.
So regular languages are closed under reversal, together with union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation, star, prefix and suffix.

scenes.title: Closure table: which classes survive which operations

steps.caption: For each class, which of five operations keep you inside it? The cells that matter are the 'no' ones. We fill the table class by class.
Regular: closed under all five. Each has a construction on DFAs and NFAs.

set.text: all five: product, flip finals, ε-arrows

steps.caption: DCFL: only complement survives (a DPDA can be completed and its answer flipped). Union fails: {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j} ∪ {aⁱbʲcᵏ : j = k} needs a guess.
CFL: union, concatenation and star combine grammars. Intersection and complement fail, because {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} ∩ {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}.
CSL: closed under all five. Closure under complement is the Immerman-Szelepcsényi theorem: nondeterministic linear space is closed under complement.
Recursive: closed under all five. For complement, run the decider and swap accept with reject.
RE: closed under all but complement. If both L and its complement were RE, L would be recursive, and the halting language is RE but not recursive.

set.text: RE is not closed under complement

steps.caption: Seven 'no' cells to remember: DCFL has four (union, intersection, concatenation, star), CFL has two (intersection, complement), RE has one (complement).

scenes.title: Deciding emptiness of a CFG by marking variables

objects.text: S → AB   A → aA | C   B → bB | b   C → CC

steps.caption: Is L(G) empty? G: S → AB, A → aA | C, B → bB | b, C → CC. Emptiness is decidable. Mark a variable if some rule for it uses only terminals and already marked variables, and repeat until nothing changes. The arrows show which variables each variable needs.
Round 1: B → b uses only a terminal, so B can produce a string. Mark B.
Round 2: A → aA needs A, which is not marked, and A → C needs C, which is not marked. C → CC needs C. S → AB needs A. Nothing new is marked, so we have reached a fixed point.
S is not marked, so S derives no terminal string. L(G) = ∅. A search over all derivations up to length 8 finds no string, which agrees.
Change A → C into A → a. Round 1 now marks A and B, since both have terminal-only rules. Round 2: S → AB uses two marked variables, so S is marked. L(G) is not empty and contains ab.

set.text: S → AB   A → aA | a   B → bB | b   C → CC

steps.caption: The same fixed-point style decides finiteness, and CYK decides membership. Equivalence, universality and ambiguity of context-free grammars are undecidable, and so is almost everything about Turing machines.
